definition: Indexed languages are a class of formal languages discovered by Alfred Aho; they are described by indexed grammars and can be recognized by nested stack automata.
details: Indexed languages are a proper subset of context-sensitive languages. They qualify as an abstract family of languages (furthermore a full AFL) and hence satisfy many closure properties. However, they are not closed under intersection or complement. The class of indexed languages has practical importance in natural language processing as a computationally affordable generalization of context-free languages, since indexed grammars can describe many of the nonlocal constraints occurring in natural languages. Gerald Gazdar (1988) and Vijayashanker (1987) introduced a mildly context-sensitive language class now known as linear indexed grammars (LIG). Linear indexed grammars have additional restrictions relative to indexed grammars. LIGs are weakly equivalent (generate the same language class) as tree adjoining grammars.

explainer.lead: Indexed languages are a class of formal languages, discovered by Alfred Aho, described by indexed grammars and recognized by nested stack automata. They matter in natural language processing as an affordable generalization of context-free languages.

tiers.eli5: It's a family of formal languages just powerful enough to handle some grammar rules that simpler language classes cannot.
tiers.practitioner: NLP engineers use them because indexed grammars describe many nonlocal constraints occurring in natural language. A pitfall is that they are not closed under intersection or complement, so combining or negating them breaks the class.
tiers.paperLevel: A proper subset of context-sensitive languages forming a full abstract family of languages (full AFL), hence satisfying many closure properties, but not closed under intersection or complement.

explainer.example: An indexed grammar capturing long-distance agreement constraints yields an indexed language that a context-free grammar cannot describe.
